screens.title: Working with Audio Assets & Sound Design
screens.narratorSegment: Sound design is a core ingredient of player experience. In this lesson you will learn how to import common audio formats, choose load types that balance memory and C P U, set up AudioSource components for 2D music and 3D sound effects, and organize audio routing with an AudioMixer. We’ll explain why WAV, MP3, and OGG behave differently in memory and C P U, and show practical rules: short frequently played effects should be loaded into memory, long background music should be streamed. You will also see how a single AudioListener acts as your scene’s ears and why multiple listeners create conflicts. Finally, we’ll outline an approachable workflow: import SFX and music into separate folders, assign sensible import settings, create an AudioMixer with Music and SFX groups, and route your sources. By the end you’ll be able to decide format and load type tradeoffs, implement a looping 2D music player, and add a 3D SFX that attenuates with distance. Think about a game you know: which sounds need instant playback, and which should stream? That question will guide your choices.

screens.title: Audio Formats: WAV vs MP3 vs OGG
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a simple claim: the audio format you choose directly affects file size, memory use, and C P U work. WAV is uncompressed PCM, offering the highest fidelity and predictable latency but large file sizes and heavy memory use. MP3 is widely supported with acceptable compression for shorter music, but its licensing history and compression artifacts can matter. OGG Vorbis offers better quality at similar sizes and is often preferred in game development. A concrete example: a two-minute background music track in WAV may be tens of megabytes and should be streamed, whereas the same track in Vorbis at moderate quality may be a fraction of the size and still streamed for memory savings. For a short UI click, a tiny WAV could be fine, but ADPCM or compressed-in-memory Vorbis reduces storage and often lowers runtime C P U overhead for short, frequently played clips. A common misconception is that compressed always equals lower C P U; in practice streaming reduces memory but can increase C P U while decompression on the fly occurs. The takeaway is to match format to role: prioritize uncompressed for tiny, critical sounds, Vorbis for general music, and streaming for long tracks. Ask yourself: will this clip be played instantly many times, or will it be a long continuous track?

keyIdea.text: WAV for tiny critical clips, Vorbis for music quality/size balance, stream long tracks to save memory.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Audio Formats
Formats at a glance
WAV (PCM)
Uncompressed. Best for tiny UI cues when absolute fidelity and predictable latency are required.
MP3
Compressed, widely supported. Good for general audio but can have compression artifacts.
OGG Vorbis
Open format with better quality-to-size tradeoff. Common choice in game builds.
Example
A two-minute music track: WAV uses much more memory and should be streamed, Vorbis reduces size while maintaining quality and is also typically streamed.
Decision guide
  • Short, frequent SFX: Decompress On Load or ADPCM to minimize playback latency.
  • Medium clips: Compressed In Memory to balance memory and CPU.
  • Long music/dialogue: Streaming to avoid loading entire file into memory.
Common misconception
Compression always saves CPU. In truth, streaming saves memory but may increase CPU during decompression. Choose based on your runtime profile.
Key Takeaway

Pick format by clip role: prioritize low-latency memory for SFX and streaming for long music.

screens.title: Load Type Options & Tradeoffs
screens.narratorSegment: Load Type controls when and how an audio clip occupies memory and C P U. Decompress On Load fully expands the clip into memory when the asset is imported or loaded, which means instant playback with minimal runtime decompression cost — ideal for very short and frequently played sounds like UI clicks. Compressed In Memory keeps the clip compressed in R A M and decompresses on the fly during playback, a compromise for medium-length clips where memory is available but you want smaller footprint. Streaming reads small chunks from disk as playback progresses. Streaming is the right choice for long background tracks or dialogue because it keeps memory low and only uses C P U for decompression as needed. A concrete example: a ten-second voiceover used occasionally could be Compressed In Memory; a five-minute ambient track should be Streaming. A common mistake is setting everything to Streaming to save memory without profiling; streaming increases disk input and output and may introduce latency on some platforms. Walk through a simple process: decide clip role, measure clip length, pick load type, test playback in editor, and profile memory and C P U. This repeatable process prevents surprises during playtests and helps you prioritize which assets to optimize first. What clip will you profile first in your project?

keyIdea.title: Pick load type by length & frequency
keyIdea.text: Decompress short sounds for instant playback, stream long tracks, and use compressed-in-memory for medium clips.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Load Types
Step-by-step decision process
  1. Identify clip role. Is it UI, SFX, dialogue, or music?
  2. Measure length. Under a few seconds favors decompressed; minutes favors streaming.
  3. Estimate frequency. If played many times per second, prefer in-memory decompression.
  4. Test and profile. Run memory and CPU checks in the target build.
Concrete example
A ten-second explanatory voiceover used occasionally: Compressed In Memory. A five-minute looped ambience: Streaming.
Quick reference
Decompress On Load
Fast playback, high memory. Use for short, critical SFX.
Compressed In Memory
Medium memory and CPU tradeoff. Good for medium-length clips.
Streaming
Low memory, higher I/O and CPU during playback. Ideal for long music and dialogue.
Key Takeaway

Use a short decision checklist: role → length → frequency → profile to choose load type safely.

screens.title: AudioSource: the in-scene speaker
screens.narratorSegment: An AudioSource is a Unity component that acts like a speaker attached to a GameObject. It holds an AudioClip and exposes properties such as Play On Awake, Loop, Volume, Pitch, Output, Spatial Blend, Min Distance, and Max Distance. Definition aside, the practical skill is knowing which properties to tweak for a given role. For background music use Play On Awake, Loop, and Spatial Blend set to zero for 2D playback routed to the Music group. For a 3D nearby explosion, uncheck Play On Awake, use a short clip with Decompress On Load, set Spatial Blend to one, and tune Min/Max Distance so the sound falls off correctly. A concrete example: for a coin pickup sound, set Decompress On Load, small Min Distance, and high volume so it reads as immediate feedback. A common beginner mistake is leaving Spatial Blend at an intermediate value when a source should be purely 2D or fully 3D; this makes positioning feel inconsistent. The takeaway: treat AudioSource as your control point for behavior, and pick properties based on whether the clip is ambient music, UI, or spatial SFX. What three properties would you tune first for your game’s footsteps?

keyIdea.title: AudioSource is behavior
keyIdea.text: Use AudioSource properties to control how and when an AudioClip plays, and whether it behaves as 2D or 3D audio.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › AudioSource
Core properties
  • AudioClip — the audio asset to play.
  • Play On Awake — plays when object activates.
  • Loop — repeats the clip.
  • Volume & Pitch — loudness and playback speed.
  • Spatial Blend — 0 = 2D, 1 = 3D.
  • Min/Max Distance — attenuation range for 3D sounds.
  • Output — route to an AudioMixer group.
Example
MusicPlayer uses Play On Awake, Loop, Spatial Blend 0, and Output set to the Music mixer group. A chest SFX uses Spatial Blend 1 and short Min/Max Distance.
Common mistakes
Leaving Spatial Blend between 0 and 1 for sounds meant to be purely UI or purely 3D, forgetting to route to an AudioMixer group so you can't adjust group volume, and attaching multiple AudioListeners to prefabs which breaks audio playback are frequent issues.
Key Takeaway

Use AudioSource settings to match the sound role: instant UI, looped music, or spatial SFX with tuned distances.

screens.title: AudioListener & Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: The AudioListener is the receiver for all audio in a Unity scene and functions like the player’s ears. Unity expects exactly one active AudioListener. Practically, you typically place it on the Main Camera or on the player GameObject so that listening follows the player. A common problem arises when imported prefabs include their own AudioListener; placing such prefabs into a scene with an existing listener produces a warning and unpredictable behavior or silence. A concrete example: when a team imports a character prefab that brings a camera and AudioListener, adding that prefab to the scene may disable or conflict with the intended listener, causing all audio to stop. The correct fix is to remove the redundant AudioListener from the prefab or disable it before runtime. Another subtle issue is forgetting to move the listener during cutscenes; if the camera changes but the listener stays, spatialized audio will feel disconnected. The takeaway is to ensure a single authoritative AudioListener that moves with the player or active camera. A quick question to check your setup: does every scene in your build have exactly one active AudioListener?

keyIdea.text: Keep one AudioListener, usually on the main camera or player, to ensure consistent spatial audio and avoid warnings.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › AudioListener
Role
Receives audio from all AudioSources. It determines what the player hears and how spatial audio is perceived.
Common Pitfall
Imported prefabs may include their own AudioListener. Having more than one causes warnings and breaks expected audio behavior.
Quick fix
Remove or disable extra AudioListeners on prefabs. Keep a single listener on the main camera or active player object.
Practical checks
  • Open the scene and search for AudioListener components.
  • If multiple exist, remove extras from prefabs or scene objects not intended to be the ears.
  • Test during camera cuts: move the listener if listening should follow the active view.
Key Takeaway

Ensure a single active AudioListener that follows the player or active camera to preserve spatial consistency.

screens.title: AudioMixer & Grouping Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: An AudioMixer provides centralized routing, effects, and volume control across many AudioSources. Think of it as a small mixing console inside Unity. The typical architecture uses a Master group with child groups such as Music and SFX. You create an AudioMixer asset, add groups under Master, and then route each AudioSource by setting its Output to the appropriate group. This lets you adjust the entire category’s volume during playtesting or apply group effects like reverb or low-pass. A concrete example: route a looping soundtrack to the Music group and all jump, collision, and UI sounds to SFX. During a tense scene you can quickly lower Music while boosting SFX without touching individual sources. A common misconception is that effects must be applied on each source; applying on a group is far more efficient and consistent. For collaborative teams, naming and structuring groups early prevents confusion later. The takeaway is to build a simple Master > Music, SFX hierarchy, route sources by category, and use group-level controls to iterate mixes quickly. Which groups will your game need beyond Music and SFX?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › AudioMixer Workflow
Mixer hierarchy
Master
› Music
› SFX
Create the AudioMixer asset, then add groups under Master. Use the inspector to add effects per group and expose volume parameters for runtime control.
Practical example
Create GameMixer, add SFX and Music groups, set AudioSource Output to the chosen group, and use the mixer faders to balance in play mode. Apply a soft reverb to ambient SFX group to glue world sounds together.
Misconception
Applying effects to individual sources is less maintainable than applying effects at the group level for consistent treatment.
Key Takeaway

Use grouped routing to simplify mixing and to enable rapid adjustments during playtests and polish passes.

screens.title: Implementing 2D Music & 3D SFX — Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough turns the concepts into a repeatable workflow. First, create folders: Assets/Audio/SFX and Assets/Audio/Music. Import your short SFX into SFX and set Load Type to Decompress On Load and Compression to ADPCM for low C P U. Import the longer music into Music and set Load Type to Streaming with Vorbis compression at an appropriate quality setting. Next, create an AudioMixer asset named GameMixer and add groups under Master for Music and SFX. To implement 2D background music, create an empty GameObject named MusicPlayer, add an AudioSource, drag the music clip into the AudioClip slot, check Play On Awake and Loop, set Spatial Blend to 0 for 2D, and set Output to the Music group. For 3D SFX, add a Cube to the scene, attach an AudioSource, put your SFX in the clip slot, set Spatial Blend to 1, and tune Min Distance and Max Distance for realistic falloff. Route that source to the SFX mixer group. Test by playing the scene, moving the camera, and adjusting group volume in the AudioMixer window. A common issue is forgetting to profile; always check memory and C P U in a build after these changes. Which step would you automate in your pipeline?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hands-on Workflow
Step checklist
  1. Create folders: Assets/Audio/SFX and Assets/Audio/Music.
  2. Import SFX: set Load Type = Decompress On Load, Compression = ADPCM.
  3. Import Music: set Load Type = Streaming, Compression = Vorbis.
  4. Create GameMixer and add Music and SFX groups.
  5. Set AudioSource Output to appropriate group and test in play mode.
Test scenario
Place MusicPlayer with looped music. Place a Cube with AudioSource for SFX and a simple collision script that plays the clip on impact. Play scene and move camera to verify 3D attenuation and group volume adjustments in the AudioMixer.
Key Takeaway
Follow a checklist: organize folders, set load types by role, route to mixer groups, then profile in a build.

screens.title: Collision-triggered SFX — Script Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: We’ll walk through a simple and robust script pattern to play a 3D sound when two objects collide. The core idea is to get the AudioSource on the same GameObject as the collider, check that the AudioSource exists in Start, then call Play when a collision event fires. In practice you add an AudioSource, set Spatial Blend to one for 3D, and configure Min and Max Distance for correct attenuation. The script checks for the component and logs an error if missing so you can catch setup errors early. A concrete example: a cube in the scene has an AudioSource with a coin pickup clip. When a falling object collides, the OnCollisionEnter method triggers audioSource. Play, producing an immediate feedback sound. A common mistake is calling Play without ensuring the clip or AudioSource exists, which leads to null-reference errors or silent failures. Another risk is repeatedly calling Play in high-frequency collisions; guard with a check for audioSource. isPlaying if you want only one overlapping instance. The takeaway is to validate components in Start and to use Unity’s collision callbacks responsibly to trigger audio. How will you guard against overlapping SFX in your project?

keyIdea.text: Validate the AudioSource in Start, handle missing components gracefully, and prevent unintended overlapping playback.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PlaySoundOnCollision.cs
Purpose
Ensure an AudioSource exists, then play a sound when a collision occurs. Guard against missing components and overlapping playback if desired.
Practical tips
  • Set Spatial Blend to 1 for a 3D SFX.
  • Use audioSource.isPlaying to avoid stacked audio in high-frequency collisions.
  • Log errors in Start if the AudioSource is missing to speed debugging.
Code (visual)
using UnityEngine;

public class PlaySoundOnCollision : MonoBehaviour
{
    private AudioSource audioSource;

    void Start()
    {
        audioSource = GetComponent();
        if (audioSource == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("AudioSource component not found on this GameObject!");
        }
    }

    void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
    {
        if (audioSource != null && !audioSource.isPlaying)
        {
            audioSource.Play();
            Debug.Log("Playing SFX!");
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway
Validate components in Start and avoid repeated Play calls when not desired to ensure robust SFX behavior.

screens.title: 3D Spatial Audio & Attenuation
screens.narratorSegment: 3D spatial audio makes sound position matter: as the listener moves, volume and panning change. Spatial Blend interpolates between 2D playback and full 3D positioning. When set to one, Unity applies attenuation using Min Distance and Max Distance. Min Distance is the radius around the source where the sound plays at full volume; Max Distance is the outer radius beyond which the sound is silent or falls to the rolloff curve. A concrete example: a campfire SFX might have a Min Distance of one meter so nearby players hear it strongly, and a Max Distance of twenty meters so it fades realistically. A common misconception is that Max Distance alone sets loudness; in reality, rolloff curves and listener movement combine to shape perceived volume. Another practical point: spatialization plugins may affect stereo width and HRTF behaviour; always test on your target platform. The takeaway is to tune Spatial Blend, Min and Max Distances for each sound role: small values for close-up interactions, larger values for ambient sources. How will you prototype attenuation values quickly in your scene? 3D Spatial Audio & Attenuation means use spatial blend with min/max distance to craft believable falloff for placed sound sources.. In practical terms, how min distance, max distance, and spatial blend shape perceived sound. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › 3D Spatial Audio
Core terms
  • Spatial Blend — mix between 2D and 3D.
  • Min Distance — full volume radius.
  • Max Distance — outer falloff limit.
  • Rolloff Curve — defines how volume decreases with distance.
Example
Place an ambient source with Min Distance 2 and Max Distance 30 to make it feel present nearby but subtle at a distance.
Testing tips
While playing the scene, move the listener object around the source and observe changes. Use the Audio window’s profiler to watch sample rates and CPU. If spatialization feels off, adjust Min/Max values, rolloff curve, or Spatialize settings.

Tune distances and spatial blend by role: close interactions need tight Min Distance, ambience needs broad Max Distance.

screens.title: Testing Audio in Play and Build
screens.narratorSegment: Audio decisions must be verified by testing in both the editor and an actual build for your target platform. Start by playing the scene in the editor and listening for correct routing, spatialization, and immediate playback behavior. Use the Audio window and Profiler to watch memory and C P U usage as clips play. For larger builds, build to device and test streaming behavior, especially on slower disks or mobile storage where streaming input and output may become a bottleneck. A concrete example: a music track that streams fine on desktop might stutter on a mobile device if disk reads are slow or decompression is expensive; in that case you may reduce music bitrate or change load type. A common misconception is that editor results mirror builds; they often do not because editor resources differ. The practical workflow: test in editor, profile, make incremental changes to settings, then test in a development build on a device. Keep a short list of assets to optimize first: the longest music track, the most frequently played SFX, and any dialogue files. The question to end on: which asset causes the largest memory spike in your project, and how will you adjust its settings?

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Step-by-step Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: This activity ties earlier topics into a concrete lab. Follow these steps: first download or gather a short SFX and a long music track and place them in Assets/Audio/SFX and Assets/Audio/Music. Import the SFX and set Load Type to Decompress On Load with ADPCM compression. Import the music and set Load Type to Streaming with Vorbis compression at around sixty percent quality to balance fidelity and size. A common failure is forgetting to route Output to the mixer group — check the AudioSource inspector if group volume controls don’t affect the sound. fullNarratorScript:
Sound design is a core ingredient of player experience. In this lesson you will learn how to import common audio formats, choose load types that balance memory and C P U, set up AudioSource components for 2D music and 3D sound effects, and organize audio routing with an AudioMixer. We’ll explain why WAV, MP3, and OGG behave differently in memory and C P U, and show practical rules: short frequently played effects should be loaded into memory, long background music should be streamed. You will also see how a single AudioListener acts as your scene’s ears and why multiple listeners create conflicts. Finally, we’ll outline an approachable workflow: import SFX and music into separate folders, assign sensible import settings, create an AudioMixer with Music and SFX groups, and route your sources. By the end you’ll be able to decide format and load type tradeoffs, implement a looping 2D music player, and add a 3D SFX that attenuates with distance. Think about a game you know: which sounds need instant playback, and which should stream? That question will guide your choices.

By the end of these exercises you will be able to import common audio file types and choose appropriate compression, configure Unity import and sample rate settings to balance quality and performance, set up AudioSource components to play both looping background music and discrete sound effects, and implement spatialized 3D audio so sounds attenuate with distance. You will also learn to manage the AudioListener properly to avoid conflicts, and to create an AudioMixer with groups so you can route and apply effects to categories like Music and SFX. Each objective builds a practical skill: importing with correct load type reduces memory spikes, configuring spatial blend and distances makes the world feel more real, and an AudioMixer gives you centralized control during playtesting. These skills let you prototype quickly and polish later without reworking asset decisions. Consider which objective you want to practice first: format choices, source configuration, spatialization, or mixing. Each one directly affects how players perceive feedback and atmosphere.

This second objectives panel focuses on practical mixing and runtime performance. You will learn to create an AudioMixer asset, create mixer groups for music and sound effects, and route AudioSources into those groups so that a single control can change many sounds at once. You will practice applying effects such as reverb or low-pass to an entire group and learn when that is preferable to changing individual sources. You will also gain a checklist for managing the AudioListener to avoid the common multi-listener mistake and a decision guide for choosing compression formats like PCM, ADPCM, or Vorbis based on clip length and C P U budget. These objectives help you work with a team: consistent mixer groups and routing make balancing easier during playtests and reduce iterative rework. Imagine adjusting the SFX volume slider mid-playtest rather than editing dozens of sources — that efficiency is what these objectives deliver.

Start with a simple claim: the audio format you choose directly affects file size, memory use, and C P U work. WAV is uncompressed PCM, offering the highest fidelity and predictable latency but large file sizes and heavy memory use. MP3 is widely supported with acceptable compression for shorter music, but its licensing history and compression artifacts can matter. OGG Vorbis offers better quality at similar sizes and is often preferred in game development. A concrete example: a two-minute background music track in WAV may be tens of megabytes and should be streamed, whereas the same track in Vorbis at moderate quality may be a fraction of the size and still streamed for memory savings. For a short UI click, a tiny WAV could be fine, but ADPCM or compressed-in-memory Vorbis reduces storage and often lowers runtime C P U overhead for short, frequently played clips. A common misconception is that compressed always equals lower C P U; in practice streaming reduces memory but can increase C P U while decompression on the fly occurs. The takeaway is to match format to role: prioritize uncompressed for tiny, critical sounds, Vorbis for general music, and streaming for long tracks. Ask yourself: will this clip be played instantly many times, or will it be a long continuous track?

Load Type controls when and how an audio clip occupies memory and C P U. Decompress On Load fully expands the clip into memory when the asset is imported or loaded, which means instant playback with minimal runtime decompression cost — ideal for very short and frequently played sounds like UI clicks. Compressed In Memory keeps the clip compressed in R A M and decompresses on the fly during playback, a compromise for medium-length clips where memory is available but you want smaller footprint. Streaming reads small chunks from disk as playback progresses. Streaming is the right choice for long background tracks or dialogue because it keeps memory low and only uses C P U for decompression as needed. A concrete example: a ten-second voiceover used occasionally could be Compressed In Memory; a five-minute ambient track should be Streaming. A common mistake is setting everything to Streaming to save memory without profiling; streaming increases disk input and output and may introduce latency on some platforms. Walk through a simple process: decide clip role, measure clip length, pick load type, test playback in editor, and profile memory and C P U. This repeatable process prevents surprises during playtests and helps you prioritize which assets to optimize first. What clip will you profile first in your project?

An AudioSource is a Unity component that acts like a speaker attached to a GameObject. It holds an AudioClip and exposes properties such as Play On Awake, Loop, Volume, Pitch, Output, Spatial Blend, Min Distance, and Max Distance. Definition aside, the practical skill is knowing which properties to tweak for a given role. For background music use Play On Awake, Loop, and Spatial Blend set to zero for 2D playback routed to the Music group. For a 3D nearby explosion, uncheck Play On Awake, use a short clip with Decompress On Load, set Spatial Blend to one, and tune Min/Max Distance so the sound falls off correctly. A concrete example: for a coin pickup sound, set Decompress On Load, small Min Distance, and high volume so it reads as immediate feedback. A common beginner mistake is leaving Spatial Blend at an intermediate value when a source should be purely 2D or fully 3D; this makes positioning feel inconsistent. The takeaway: treat AudioSource as your control point for behavior, and pick properties based on whether the clip is ambient music, UI, or spatial SFX. What three properties would you tune first for your game’s footsteps?

The AudioListener is the receiver for all audio in a Unity scene and functions like the player’s ears. Unity expects exactly one active AudioListener. Practically, you typically place it on the Main Camera or on the player GameObject so that listening follows the player. A common problem arises when imported prefabs include their own AudioListener; placing such prefabs into a scene with an existing listener produces a warning and unpredictable behavior or silence. A concrete example: when a team imports a character prefab that brings a camera and AudioListener, adding that prefab to the scene may disable or conflict with the intended listener, causing all audio to stop. The correct fix is to remove the redundant AudioListener from the prefab or disable it before runtime. Another subtle issue is forgetting to move the listener during cutscenes; if the camera changes but the listener stays, spatialized audio will feel disconnected. The takeaway is to ensure a single authoritative AudioListener that moves with the player or active camera. A quick question to check your setup: does every scene in your build have exactly one active AudioListener?

An AudioMixer provides centralized routing, effects, and volume control across many AudioSources. Think of it as a small mixing console inside Unity. The typical architecture uses a Master group with child groups such as Music and SFX. You create an AudioMixer asset, add groups under Master, and then route each AudioSource by setting its Output to the appropriate group. This lets you adjust the entire category’s volume during playtesting or apply group effects like reverb or low-pass. A concrete example: route a looping soundtrack to the Music group and all jump, collision, and UI sounds to SFX. During a tense scene you can quickly lower Music while boosting SFX without touching individual sources. A common misconception is that effects must be applied on each source; applying on a group is far more efficient and consistent. For collaborative teams, naming and structuring groups early prevents confusion later. The takeaway is to build a simple Master > Music, SFX hierarchy, route sources by category, and use group-level controls to iterate mixes quickly. Which groups will your game need beyond Music and SFX?

This walkthrough turns the concepts into a repeatable workflow. First, create folders: Assets/Audio/SFX and Assets/Audio/Music. Import your short SFX into SFX and set Load Type to Decompress On Load and Compression to ADPCM for low C P U. Import the longer music into Music and set Load Type to Streaming with Vorbis compression at an appropriate quality setting. Next, create an AudioMixer asset named GameMixer and add groups under Master for Music and SFX.
